idiom_name: ROM (Ruby Object Mapper): relations read rows, mappers build plain structs
implementation_notes: Ruby's data-mapping toolkit is ROM: relations read the database, a mapper per relation converts tuples into plain structs, and commands/repositories are the write side, so domain objects contain no SQL and no schema knowledge. This is a deliberate departure from the default Rails stack, where ActiveRecord is an Active Record implementation that most gems assume; the same niche was previously filled by the DataMapper gem. Adopt ROM when the model must survive schema changes or be shared across stores, and expect to wire relations, mappers and the container explicitly at the application boundary instead of relying on convention.
code_sketch:
require "rom"

rom = ROM.container(:sql, "sqlite://app.db") do |config|
  config.relation(:customers) { schema(infer: true) }   # reading half: relations
end

customers = rom.relations[:customers]
# rows arrive as plain structs (ROM::Struct), never as objects carrying SQL methods
customers.where(id: 42).one                             # => struct(id: 42, name: "Ada")
# writes go through commands/repositories; the domain class stays persistence-ignorant
pitfalls: ROM structs are static read models: attribute assignment is not a tracked change and raises, so writes must go through commands or repositories - code that assumes ActiveRecord's setters breaks loudly.
Rails plugins and gems assume ActiveRecord; running both stacks means two connection pools, two transaction concepts and migrations that only one side knows about.
Auto-struct infers structs from the schema, so once you map to your own domain classes the mapper must be maintained next to every relation it serves.
